If they refuse, call the Consumer Protection Division at 1-877-880-5550. If you settle through mediation, your rights for that dispute end, so only accept a deal you are happy with. Small claims court is the last step, and you won't be ordered to pay their costs unless your claim was frivolous or vexatious.
rules.script_hint: Under section 28 of Saskatchewan's Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act, please repair this free of charge within a reasonable time, or, because the fault is serious, refund the purchase price.
rules.source_quote: the party in breach shall, within a reasonable period, make good the breach free of charge to the consumer

rules.title: Saskatchewan: the store stands behind the written warranty that came with the item
rules.window_note: Lasts as long as the written warranty does. The store is only off the hook if it told you in writing, before you bought, that it does not take on that warranty. It doesn't matter whether you knew about the warranty or relied on it when you bought. The Act counts service contracts, such as extended warranties, as written warranties too.
rules.what_you_get: If a written warranty came with or was attached to the item, the store that sold it is treated as a warrantor too, so it can't just send you to the maker. If a valid repair or replacement claim isn't done within a reasonable time, you can have it fixed elsewhere and recover the reasonable cost and other foreseeable losses from the warrantor. If the warranty covers only some parts or some costs, you don't have to pay extra repair costs unless you agreed in writing to pay them.
rules.how_to_claim: Take the item back to the store with your receipt and the warranty. If they say 'call the manufacturer', say section 24 of The Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act makes them a warrantor too, unless they told you otherwise in writing before the sale. If the repair isn't done within a reasonable time, have it fixed elsewhere and claim the cost under section 32. If they refuse, call the Consumer Protection Division at 1-877-880-5550, then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 24 of Saskatchewan's Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act makes you, the store, a warrantor under the written warranty that came with this, so please arrange the repair.
rules.source_quote: If an additional written warranty accompanies or is attached to a consumer product sold by a retail seller, the retail seller is deemed to be a warrantor respecting the additional written warranty

rules.title: Saskatchewan: what the store, the maker or an ad promised counts as a warranty
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months; it lasts as long as the promise says or suggests. A promise in the maker's own ad binds the maker, and binds the store only if the store adopted it. Promises on the label or box bind the store unless it made clear before the sale that it does not adopt them. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: Any promise or statement of fact about the item's quality, condition, performance, use or care, made by the store, the maker or their staff, in person, in writing or in an ad, is a warranty if it would usually get a reasonable person to buy. It doesn't matter whether you actually relied on it, and you can prove a spoken promise even if the written contract says something different. No such promise can cut down your statutory warranties. If the item doesn't live up to it, you get the same fix-or-refund remedies as for the statutory warranties.
rules.how_to_claim: Write down exactly what was promised, by whom and when, and keep any ad, listing or box. Go back to the store (or to the maker, for the maker's own promise) and say section 16 of The Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act makes it an express warranty. Ask for a free repair, or a refund if the item is seriously different from the promise. If they refuse, call the Consumer Protection Division at 1-877-880-5550, then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: You told me this would [what was promised], and section 16 of Saskatchewan's Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act makes that an express warranty, so please make it good.
rules.source_quote: is deemed to be an express warranty if it would usually induce a reasonable consumer to buy the consumer product, whether or not the consumer actually relies on the warranty

rules.title: Manitoba: what you buy from a business has to be of sellable quality, whatever the fine print says
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months; it's judged case by case. It doesn't cover defects the seller described to you. On a cash sale, a note about defects only counts if it was in writing and either shown clearly at or before the sale or handed to you before you accepted the item. On a credit sale it has to be in the credit agreement. For goods described as used, their age and the fact they are used are taken into account. Covers things bought from a business for personal use, not from a private seller or for a business. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: A condition built into every retail sale in Manitoba that the item is of merchantable quality, meaning free of defects apart from ones that were described to you. It applies 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary', so 'as is' or 'no warranty' fine print can't take it away. It is the seller's promise, so it's the store you hold to it.
rules.how_to_claim: Go back to the store that sold it, with your receipt. Say section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes merchantable quality a condition of the sale, and ask in writing for a repair, replacement or refund. If they refuse, either of you can ask Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office to mediate: 204-945-3800, 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba, or consumers@gov.mb.ca. If that fails, you can take the seller to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes it a condition of this sale that the item is of merchantable quality, whatever the receipt says, and it isn't, so please repair, replace or refund it.
rules.source_quote: A condition that the goods are of merchantable quality, except for such defects as are described.

rules.title: Manitoba: unless you were told it was used, it has to be new
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months, but raise it as soon as you notice signs of earlier use. A note that the item is not new only counts if it was in writing and either shown clearly at or before the sale or handed to you before you accepted it. On a purchase on credit it has to be in the credit agreement. For a vehicle, stating it is more than a year old is enough to describe it as used. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: A condition of every retail sale that the item is new and unused, unless it was described otherwise. A demo model, or something someone else already used, sold to you without being described as used breaks that condition. A contract term saying otherwise can't take it away.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the store in writing that the item shows signs of earlier use, that it wasn't described as used, and that section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes 'new and unused' a condition of the sale. Ask for a new one or your money back. If they refuse, ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate (204-945-3800, or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba), then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: This wasn't described as used, so under section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act it had to be new and unused, and it isn't; please give me a new one or a refund.
rules.source_quote: A condition that the goods are new and unused unless otherwise described; but in the case of a motor vehicle a description showing that it is more than one year old is sufficient to describe it as used.

rules.title: Manitoba: if you relied on the seller's advice for a job, the item has to be fit for it
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months. Applies when you told the seller the particular use you needed it for, relied on the seller's skill or judgment, and it's the kind of thing the seller normally sells. It doesn't apply to a sale of a specific item under its patent or trade name. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: A condition of the sale that the item is reasonably fit for the use you described, whether or not the seller made it. Fine print can't take it away.
rules.how_to_claim: Go back to the store with your receipt. Remind them what you said you needed it for and that you relied on their advice. Say section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes fitness for that use a condition of the sale, and ask for a repair, replacement or refund. If they refuse, ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate (204-945-3800, or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba), then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: I told you I needed this for [use] and relied on your advice, so section 58 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes it a condition that it's reasonably fit for that, and it isn't.
rules.source_quote: a condition that the goods are reasonably fit for the purpose; but in the case of a contract for the sale of a specified article under its patent or other trade name, there is no implied condition

rules.title: Manitoba: go back to the store for warranty repairs, even under the maker's warranty
rules.window_note: Lasts as long as the warranty you're claiming under: the maker's written term, or a reasonable time for the warranties the law builds in. Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office says that if the seller has gone out of business, you contact the maker about warranty repairs.
rules.what_you_get: The store that sold it is personally liable to you for every warranty that applies to the sale. Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office says that means you go back to the store for warranty repairs, even under the maker's warranty. The store also has to pay the expenses that come with getting the item serviced under any warranty, whether the maker, the store or someone else gave it. That doesn't mean it pays for parts or labour the warranty itself leaves out. The Consumer Protection Office warns that if a warranty covers parts but not labour, you may have to pay for the labour. Each time the store fixes a fault the Act makes it correct, it must give you a written record of every part and service used.
rules.how_to_claim: Take warranty problems back to the store you bought from, not just the maker. Say section 58.1 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes the store personally liable for the warranties on the sale, and makes it pay the expenses that come with warranty service. Ask for the written repair record that section 58(9) requires. If they refuse, contact the Consumer Protection Office: 204-945-3800, 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba, or consumers@gov.mb.ca.
rules.script_hint: Section 58.1 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes you, the seller, personally liable for the warranties on this sale and responsible for the expenses of having it serviced under the manufacturer's warranty, so please take care of this repair.
rules.source_quote: the seller shall bear all expenses incidental to having the goods serviced under any warranty whether given by the manufacturer, seller or a third party

rules.title: Manitoba: if a store sold you an extended warranty, the store has to make sure it's honoured
rules.window_note: For as long as the extended warranty or service plan you bought runs.
rules.what_you_get: The store that sold you a service or extended warranty contract is liable to you for everything it promises, even if another company runs it and even if the store isn't a party to it. That holds whether or not the store earned a fee or commission on it. The salesperson isn't personally on the hook; the store is.
rules.how_to_claim: If the warranty company stalls or says no, go back to the store that sold you the plan, with the plan paperwork and your receipt. Say section 58.2 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes the store liable for carrying out the plan, whoever runs it. If they refuse, ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate (204-945-3800, or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba), then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: You sold me this extended warranty, and section 58.2 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes you liable for the repairs it promises even though another company runs it.
rules.source_quote: the seller of the contract is liable to the buyer for the performance of all obligations under the contract to service or repair the goods, whether or not the seller is a party to the contract

rules.title: Manitoba: what the seller or its ads said about the item counts as a warranty
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months; it lasts as long as the statement promised or suggested. A spoken promise counts, but it can be hard to prove, so ask for it in writing. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: Every spoken or written statement by the seller or its staff about the item's quality, condition, quantity, performance or efficacy, whether in an ad or said to you, is an express warranty. If the item doesn't live up to it, you can hold the seller to it, on top of the warranties the law builds into every retail sale.
rules.how_to_claim: Write down what was said, who said it and when, and keep the ad or listing. Go back to the store and say section 58(8) of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes that statement an express warranty. Ask for a repair, replacement or refund. If they refuse, ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate (204-945-3800, or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba), then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Your salesperson told me this would [what was said], and under section 58(8) of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act that's an express warranty, so please make it right.
rules.source_quote: Under The Consumer Protection Act, every oral or written statement of a seller or salesperson about quality, condition, quantity or performance is an express warranty.

rules.title: Manitoba: a faulty item lets you claim money for the fault, even after you've accepted it
rules.window_note: No fixed number of months. Refusing the item outright is only possible in some cases, and only before you've accepted it. You haven't accepted goods you hadn't seen until you've had a reasonable chance to check them; telling the seller you accept, or keeping it past a reasonable time without saying you reject it, counts as accepting. If you do refuse it, you don't have to bring it back; telling the seller is enough. After you've accepted it, the claim is for money. You have two years from when you discover the problem to start a court claim.
rules.what_you_get: When a sale breaks a warranty or condition, you can take the loss off what you still owe the seller, or sue the seller for it. For poor quality, the loss is usually the gap between what the item was worth when delivered and what it would have been worth without the fault. Other losses that flow naturally from the fault can be claimed too.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the seller describing the fault and what it is costing you, such as a repair quote. Ask them to fix it, replace it or pay you the difference. If you still owe money on it, you can set the loss against what you owe. If they refuse, ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate (204-945-3800, or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba), then claim the amount in small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Under section 54 of Manitoba's Sale of Goods Act the fault in this item entitles me to the drop in its value, so please repair it, replace it or pay me that difference.
rules.source_quote: such loss is prima facie the difference between the value of the goods at the time of delivery to the buyer and the value they would have had if they had answered to the warranty

rules.title: Manitoba: either side can ask the Consumer Protection Office to mediate a warranty dispute
rules.window_note: No set deadline to ask. It only works if the business is willing to take part, and the office can't impose a settlement or guarantee the result. Keep the two-year deadline for a court claim in mind while it runs.
rules.what_you_get: An informal, confidential way to settle a warranty dispute with a seller. You or the seller can refer it to the director, who must try to settle it by mediation. An officer contacts the business, asks for its response and tells you what it said, and this goes on until you reach an agreement or a dead end. If there's no agreement, either side can take it to court.
rules.how_to_claim: First raise the problem with the seller in writing. If you're stuck, contact the Consumer Protection Office at 204-945-3800, 1-800-782-0067 toll-free in Manitoba, or consumers@gov.mb.ca. Say what you bought and when, what's wrong, what the business said and what you want. Keep copies of your receipt, the warranty and any letters.
rules.script_hint: I'd like to settle this with you, but if we can't agree I'll refer this warranty dispute to Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office for mediation under section 58(10) of the Consumer Protection Act.
rules.source_quote: as to any condition or warranty, either or both parties may refer the dispute to the director who shall endeavour by mediation to settle the dispute

rules.title: Manitoba: you don't have to mail in a warranty card to be covered
rules.window_note: Applies for as long as the warranty itself runs. Keep your bill of sale and delivery slip, since they prove the date you bought it.
rules.what_you_get: Your warranty still counts even if you never registered the product or sent back the card. The card just gives the maker a record of your purchase.
rules.how_to_claim: Claim as normal. If you're told you never registered, show your bill of sale or delivery slip as proof of the purchase date, and say Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office says registration isn't needed. You can also take the claim to the store, which answers for all warranties on the sale. If they still refuse, contact the Consumer Protection Office at 204-945-3800 or consumers@gov.mb.ca.
rules.script_hint: Manitoba's Consumer Protection Office says I don't have to register or return a warranty card to get warranty protection, so here's my bill of sale showing the purchase date.
rules.source_quote: Under Manitoba law, you don’t have to register or return a warranty card to get express warranty protection.

rules.title: Manitoba: car repairs come with a 90-day or 5,000 km warranty on parts and labour
rules.window_note: 90 days or 5,000 kilometres, whichever comes first, counted from the day the repaired vehicle is handed back to you. It covers the new or reconditioned parts the shop installed and the labour to install them, not damage from misuse or abuse. It doesn't apply to repairs paid for under an MPI insurance claim. The shop can give you longer, and your invoice has to show the warranty terms.
rules.what_you_get: The shop that repaired your vehicle is treated by law as guaranteeing the new or reconditioned parts it put in and the work to install them. If one fails within that time, you can hold the shop to that warranty. If the shop used a subcontractor, both are responsible, and the shop must tell you how to reach the subcontractor. This is on top of the other warranties the Act gives you.
rules.how_to_claim: Take the vehicle back to the shop that did the work, with your invoice, as soon as the problem shows up, and note the date and odometer reading. Say section 222 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act gives a 90-day or 5,000 km warranty on the parts and labour. If the shop refuses, contact the Consumer Protection Office at 204-945-3800 or 1-800-782-0067 toll-free, then small claims court.
rules.script_hint: You repaired my vehicle less than 90 days and 5,000 km ago, and section 222 of Manitoba's Consumer Protection Act makes you warrant those parts and the labour, so please fix this under that warranty.
rules.source_quote: Unless another term is prescribed by regulation, the term of the warranty is 90 days or 5,000 kilometres, whichever comes first.

rules.title: New Brunswick: it has to be the quality you'd expect, and fit for the job you described
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. Quality is judged by how the seller described it, the price and everything else about the sale. It doesn't cover a fault you knew about, or one the seller told you about, before you bought. On a used item you looked over first, it doesn't cover faults that looking it over should have shown you. Covers things bought, traded or leased from a business that sells that kind of item, new or used, but not from a private seller.
rules.what_you_get: A promise from the seller, built into every sale, that the item is the quality and condition you'd reasonably expect for its normal use, and that it meets all required federal and provincial health, safety and quality standards. It also has to be unused, unless you were told otherwise or it was clear it wasn't. If you told the seller what you needed it for and relied on their advice, it has to be reasonably fit for that job. A store or maker warranty can't take these promises away, and you can claim money for losses the fault caused that could have been foreseen.
rules.how_to_claim: Go back to the seller first, in writing, and give them a fair chance to fix it, unless the fault is major or giving them that chance would be a real hassle for you. Name section 10 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act. If they ask for it back, return it to them or a repair shop they run or approve; they pay your reasonable costs of doing that. If they won't help, call New Brunswick's Financial and Consumer Services Commission, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Under section 10 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act this had to be the quality you'd reasonably expect for its normal use, and it isn't, so I'm asking you to repair or replace it.
rules.source_quote: that the product is of such quality, in such state or condition, and as fit for the purpose or purposes for which products of that kind are normally used as it is reasonable to expect

rules.title: New Brunswick: if the seller doesn't fix a fault, you can hand it back for your money
rules.window_note: Two clocks. You have to find the fault within 60 days of delivery, and then reject the item within a reasonable time of finding it. For a major fault you can still reject it after 60 days, within a reasonable time of when you should have noticed. Before you reject it, give the seller a fair chance to fix it, unless the fault is major or that would be a real hassle for you. Doesn't apply to things you bought for a business, or to an item that came as part of a service or labour job, like an installation.
rules.what_you_get: All your payments back, including finance charges you reasonably paid, plus money for other losses the fault caused that could have been foreseen. The seller can hold back a fair amount for the use you got out of it, or for damage beyond normal wear and tear. You can keep the item until you're paid, and the seller pays your reasonable costs of returning it. You don't have to bring back something too big, heavy or built-in to move easily.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the seller in writing what's wrong and give them a fair chance to fix it. If they don't, write again saying you reject the item under section 16 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act and want all your payments back. Your rejection only counts once the seller knows about it, so keep proof you sent it. Hold on to the item until you're paid. If they refuse, call New Brunswick's Financial and Consumer Services Commission, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: You haven't fixed the fault, so under section 16 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act I'm rejecting this product and asking for all my payments back.
rules.source_quote: the buyer may reject the product if he does so within a reasonable time after he discovers the breach and he discovers the breach not later than sixty days after delivery of the product.

rules.title: New Brunswick: what the seller told you, or printed on the box, is a promise they must keep
rules.window_note: No cut-off of its own; a promise with a time limit lasts that long. It covers what the seller or its staff said before or when you bought, anything written on the product, its box, a label, tag or sign, and the seller's ads. Something said out loud counts unless it's clear you didn't rely on it, or it wasn't reasonable to. If a warranty says they'll repair or replace it if it breaks, the law reads that as a promise it won't break during that time.
rules.what_you_get: The seller has to stand behind those statements as part of your deal, even if the written contract says something different. The Act's usual remedies apply: a chance for them to fix it, money for the loss it caused, and, if you find the problem within 60 days of delivery or it's a major fault, the right to hand it back for your money. The seller can only limit those remedies if the limit is fair and reasonable, and never for a promise that was part of how the item was described. A store or maker warranty never cuts down the protections the law already gives you.
rules.how_to_claim: Write down exactly what you were told, by whom and when, and keep screenshots of the ad or photos of the box or label. Write to the seller, quote the promise, and say it is an express warranty under section 4 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act. Ask them to make it right. If they refuse, call New Brunswick's Financial and Consumer Services Commission, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Your staff told me [what they said], and under section 4 of New Brunswick's Consumer Product Warranty and Liability Act that is a warranty you have to honour.
rules.source_quote: any oral statement in relation to the product that the seller makes to the buyer, unless the circumstances show that the buyer does not rely, or that it is unreasonable for him to rely, on the seller’s statement

rules.title: Nova Scotia: what you buy has to last a reasonable time, by law
rules.window_note: No fixed number of years. It's judged by how that kind of item is normally used and everything else about the sale. It covers things you buy from a business for your own use, not from a private seller and not for a business. Court time limits still apply, so don't sit on it.
rules.what_you_get: A condition, built into every consumer sale, that the item will stay durable for a reasonable time. It applies whatever your contract says, and any written term that tries to cancel it or cap what you can claim is void.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the seller. Say what you paid, how long it lasted, and that section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act says goods must be durable for a reasonable period of time. Ask for a repair, a replacement or your money back. If they refuse, call Service Nova Scotia, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act says goods must be durable for a reasonable period of time, and this wasn't, so I'm asking you to repair, replace or refund it.
rules.source_quote: a condition that the goods shall be durable for a reasonable period of time having regard to the use to which they would normally be put and to all the surrounding circumstances of the sale.

rules.title: Nova Scotia: it has to be good quality, match its description, and be new unless you were told it's used
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. The quality promise doesn't cover defects the seller described to you before you bought. The 'fit for your job' promise only applies if you told the seller what you needed it for and relied on their advice, and not when you asked for a specific item by its brand or trade name. Covers things you buy from a business for your own use, not from a private seller.
rules.what_you_get: Conditions built into every consumer sale: the item is of sellable quality (the law says 'merchantable'), matches how it was described, is new and unused unless you were told otherwise, and is reasonably fit for the job you told the seller about. They apply whatever your contract says.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the seller and say which promise was broken, naming section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act. Ask for a repair, a replacement or your money back. If they refuse, call Service Nova Scotia, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act makes it a condition of my purchase that this is of merchantable quality, and it isn't, so please repair, replace or refund it.
rules.source_quote: a condition that the goods are of merchantable quality, except for such defects as are described; (i) a condition that the goods, whether bought by description or otherwise, are new and unused unless otherwise described

rules.title: Nova Scotia: 'no warranty' fine print is void, and money it cost you can be won back
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. It covers any written term or note, in the contract or not, that says the law's conditions don't apply, weakens them, or caps what the seller owes you. The rest of your contract still stands without it.
rules.what_you_get: Any such term is void. It can't be used as proof that you agreed to give up your rights, and any money you paid because of it can be won back in court.
rules.how_to_claim: If a seller points to a receipt, sign or contract that says there's no warranty to turn down your claim, tell them in writing that section 28 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act makes that term void. If you paid for a fix or a fee because of it, ask for that money back. If they refuse, call Service Nova Scotia, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 28 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act says a written term that takes away the Act's conditions or warranties is void, so the 'no warranty' line on my receipt doesn't apply.
rules.source_quote: any liability of the seller including any limitation, modification or abrogation of damages for breach of any of the conditions or warranties set out in this Act or the regulations, is void.

rules.title: Nova Scotia: a repair or other service you pay for has to be done properly
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. It covers services you pay a business for as a consumer, like a repair or an installation, but not work bought for a business.
rules.what_you_get: A condition, built into the deal, that the work will be done in a skilful, efficient and competent way. It applies whatever the work order says, and a written term that takes it away is void.
rules.how_to_claim: Go back to whoever did the work and explain what went wrong. Ask them in writing to redo it properly at no charge, or to refund what you paid for the bad work, and name section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act. If they refuse, call Service Nova Scotia, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 26 of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act says services I pay for must be performed in a skilful, efficient and competent manner, and this repair wasn't, so please redo it at no charge.
rules.source_quote: There shall be implied in every consumer sale of services a condition, on the part of the seller, that the services sold shall be performed in a skilful, efficient and competent manner.

rules.title: Nova Scotia: a car's warranty passes to the next owner, and no one can charge to transfer it
rules.window_note: Lasts as long as the car's warranty does; this law doesn't add time. It covers a warranty in the written sale or lease contract, and one the maker, seller or leasing company made to the public, like in an ad, for a car it then sold or leased.
rules.what_you_get: If you buy or lease a car second-hand, you get the same rights under its existing warranty as the first owner had. Nobody can charge you a fee to transfer it. A warranty promised in an ad counts as part of the car's sale or lease contract.
rules.how_to_claim: Contact whoever gave the warranty, usually the maker through one of its dealers, and ask for the covered repair. If they say the warranty didn't pass to you, or ask for a transfer fee, point to section 28A of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act. If they still refuse, call Service Nova Scotia, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Under section 28A of Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act I have the same rights under this car's warranty as the first owner, and no fee can be charged to transfer it.
rules.source_quote: each subsequent purchaser or lessee who acquires an ownership or leasehold interest in the automobile has the same rights and remedies under the express warranty

rules.title: Nova Scotia: online order 30 days late? Cancel it and get all your money back
rules.window_note: For online orders of $50 or more from a business. If your order gave a delivery date, or you later agreed on a new one, you can cancel once it's more than 30 days past that date, as long as it still hasn't arrived. If no date was given, the 30 days count from the day you ordered. It doesn't cover things you download or stream straight away. If they tried to deliver and you refused it, or nobody was home after fair notice, it counts as delivered.
rules.what_you_get: The seller has to refund everything you paid, including for any related purchase, within 15 days of your cancelling. If they don't, you can sue for it as a debt, or ask your credit card company to reverse the charge and any interest. The card company must do that within two billing cycles or 90 days, whichever comes first.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the seller you're cancelling, in a way you can prove later, such as email, and say it's under Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act and its Internet Sales Contract Regulations. If the item arrives after that, send it back unused within 15 days; the seller pays the reasonable cost. No refund after 15 days? Write to your credit card company with your name, card number and expiry date, the seller's name, the order date, the amount charged, what you ordered, and why, when and how you cancelled. If you're stuck, call Service Nova Scotia.
rules.script_hint: My order still hasn't arrived more than 30 days after the delivery date you gave, so I'm cancelling it under Nova Scotia's Consumer Protection Act and Internet Sales Contract Regulations and expect a full refund within 15 days.
rules.source_quote: in the case of goods, the supplier does not deliver the goods within 30 days from the delivery date specified in the contract

rules.title: Prince Edward Island: a store's goods have to be sellable quality and fit for the job you described
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. The quality promise applies when you buy from a seller who deals in that kind of item, and doesn't cover defects you should have spotted if you looked it over first. The 'fit for your job' promise needs you to have told the seller what you needed it for and relied on their judgment; it doesn't apply if you asked for a specific item by its brand or trade name. PEI law lets a seller and buyer agree to drop these promises, so check your receipt and contract. Once you've accepted the item, the law treats a fault as a claim for money, not a return.
rules.what_you_get: Money from the seller for your loss. For a quality problem, the law measures it as the gap between what the item was worth when you got it and what it would have been worth if it had been up to standard. You can knock that off anything you still owe, and still claim more if the fault caused other damage.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the seller. Say what's wrong, and that section 16 of Prince Edward Island's Sale of Goods Act makes sellable ('merchantable') quality a condition of the sale. Ask for a repair, a replacement or money to cover the loss. If they refuse, call PEI's Consumer Services office, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 16 of Prince Edward Island's Sale of Goods Act says goods bought from a seller who deals in them must be of merchantable quality, and this isn't, so please repair or replace it or pay me for the loss.
rules.source_quote: where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description, whether he be the manufacturer or not, there is an implied condition that the goods are of merchantable quality

rules.title: Prince Edward Island: sold on a false claim? You have 6 months to cancel the deal
rules.window_note: Six months from the day you made the deal. Give the business written notice within that time, by hand or by registered mail (mail counts from the day you send it). It covers claims like: the item is new when it's used or refurbished, it's a model or quality it isn't, a part or repair is needed when it isn't, or you have no rights when you do. What they said out loud counts, even if the contract says something different.
rules.what_you_get: You can cancel the deal and get your money back, and claim damages too. If the deal can't be undone, you get back what you paid above the item's fair value, or damages, or both. Whoever made the false claim is on the hook along with the business you bought from. If the seller took unfair advantage of you, a court can add punitive damages. You can't sign away this right.
rules.how_to_claim: Within six months, write to the business. Say what they told you that wasn't true, and that you're cancelling the deal under section 4 of Prince Edward Island's Business Practices Act. Hand it over or send it by registered mail, and keep proof. If they refuse, call PEI's Consumer Services office, then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: You told me [the claim that wasn't true], which is an unfair practice under Prince Edward Island's Business Practices Act, so I'm cancelling this purchase under section 4 and asking for my money back.
rules.source_quote: A remedy conferred by subsection (1) may be claimed by the giving of notice of the claim by the consumer in writing to each other party to the agreement within six months after the agreement is entered into.

rules.title: Newfoundland and Labrador: a store's goods have to be sellable quality and fit for the job you described
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. The quality promise applies when you buy from a seller who deals in that kind of item, and doesn't cover defects you should have spotted if you looked it over first. The 'fit for your job' promise needs you to have told the seller what you needed it for and relied on their judgment; it doesn't apply if you asked for a specific item by its brand or trade name. The law lets a seller and buyer agree to drop these promises, so check your receipt and contract. Once you've accepted the item, the law treats a fault as a claim for money, not a return.
rules.what_you_get: Money from the seller for your loss. For a quality problem, the law measures it as the gap between what the item was worth when you got it and what it would have been worth if it had been up to standard. You can knock that off anything you still owe, and still claim more if the fault caused other damage.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the seller. Say what's wrong, and that section 16 of Newfoundland and Labrador's Sale of Goods Act makes sellable ('merchantable') quality a condition of the sale. Ask for a repair, a replacement or money to cover the loss. If they refuse, contact the province's consumer protection office (Consumer and Financial Services, Government Services), then go to small claims court.
rules.script_hint: Section 16 of Newfoundland and Labrador's Sale of Goods Act says goods bought from a seller who deals in them must be of merchantable quality, and this isn't, so please repair or replace it or pay me for the loss.
rules.source_quote: where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description, whether he or she is the manufacturer or not, there is an implied condition that the goods shall be of merchantable quality

rules.title: Newfoundland and Labrador: misled about what you bought? A court can undo the sale
rules.window_note: The act sets no deadline of its own, but general court time limits apply, so don't wait. It covers claims like: the item is new when it's used or refurbished, it's a quality or model it isn't, a part or repair is needed when it isn't, repairs were done when they weren't, or you have no rights when you do. It counts whether it happened before, during or after the sale.
rules.what_you_get: A court can cancel the sale, order your money back, and award damages, including punitive damages. The business has to prove it didn't act unfairly, not the other way round. You can't sign these rights away.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the business, say what they told you that wasn't true, and ask them to cancel the sale and refund you. If they won't, file a complaint with the province's consumer protection office (Consumer and Financial Services, Government Services), which can try to settle it. If you go to court, the law says you must also send a copy of your claim to the Director of Consumer Protection and Business Practices.
rules.script_hint: What you told me about this item wasn't true, which is an unfair business practice under section 7 of Newfoundland and Labrador's Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act, so I'm asking you to cancel the sale and refund me.
rules.source_quote: Where a consumer has suffered damage as a result of an unfair business practice or unconscionable act or practice, the consumer may start an action against a supplier.

rules.title: Newfoundland and Labrador: online or phone order 30 days late? Cancel it for a full refund
rules.window_note: For orders made online, by phone or by mail, where you couldn't see the item first. If your contract gave a delivery date, you can cancel once it's more than 30 days past that date, as long as it hasn't arrived. If no date was given, the 30 days count from the day you ordered. You can also cancel within 30 days of ordering if the seller never sent you a copy of the contract within 15 days.
rules.what_you_get: The seller must refund everything you paid, with no deductions, within 15 days of your cancelling. If it doesn't, you can ask your credit card company to reverse the charge and any interest. The card company must do that within two billing cycles or 90 days, whichever comes first.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the seller you're cancelling, in a way you can prove later, such as email. If the item turns up after that, send it back unused within 15 days in a way that gives you proof of delivery; the seller pays the reasonable cost. No refund after 15 days? Write to your credit card company with the seller's name, the order date, the amount charged, what you ordered, and why, when and how you cancelled. If you're stuck, contact the province's consumer protection office (Consumer and Financial Services, Government Services).
rules.script_hint: My order is more than 30 days past its delivery date and still hasn't arrived, so I'm cancelling it under section 32 of Newfoundland and Labrador's Consumer Protection and Business Practices Act and expect a full refund within 15 days.
rules.source_quote: before the goods or services are delivered where the goods or services to be delivered under the contract are not delivered to the consumer within 30 days of the supply date

rules.title: Mexico: a warranty can't be shorter than 90 days
rules.window_note: At least 90 days from the day the item was delivered to you. That is the legal minimum for anything sold with a warranty; if the warranty card (póliza) gives you longer, the longer time counts.
rules.what_you_get: A warranty that lasts at least 90 days. The seller must hand you a written póliza when you get the item, saying what it covers, how long it lasts, its conditions, how to claim, the address for claims and where the repair shops are.
rules.how_to_claim: Find the póliza and your receipt. Take the item to the store where you bought it, or to the place the póliza names, and ask for the repair under the warranty. If they refuse, call Profeco's Teléfono del Consumidor on 800 468 8722 (55 5568 8722 in Mexico City) or file a complaint at a Profeco office.
rules.script_hint: Article 77 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor says a warranty can't be shorter than 90 days from delivery, so this is still covered; please honour the warranty.
rules.source_quote: la garantía no podrá ser inferior a noventa días contados a partir de la entrega del bien o la prestación del servicio.

rules.title: Mexico: household appliances must come with at least a 1-year warranty
rules.window_note: At least 1 year for electric household appliances, like fridges, washing machines, microwaves, blenders and vacuums. Other electric and electronic products get at least 3 months. It counts from the day you received it, or, if it had to be installed, from the day it was installed and working in your home. The póliza can give you longer.
rules.what_you_get: A warranty of at least one year on an electric household appliance, under Mexico's official standard for electronics and appliance warranties (NOM-024-SCFI-2013). For that whole time the warranty has to cover all parts and labour.
rules.how_to_claim: Take the appliance and its stamped póliza, or your receipt, to the store or service centre the póliza names, or call the maker's service line printed on it. If they say the warranty is shorter than a year, point to NOM-024-SCFI-2013 and ask for the repair. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Mexico's official standard NOM-024-SCFI-2013 says a household appliance's warranty can't be shorter than one year, so this is still covered; please repair it at no cost.
rules.source_quote: Duración de la garantía, la cual no puede ser menor a tres meses para el caso de productos eléctricos y electrónicos y, para el caso de electrodomésticos, no puede ser menor de un año.

rules.title: Mexico: the maker, the importer and the seller all have to honour the warranty
rules.window_note: For as long as the warranty lasts: at least 90 days from delivery, or longer if the póliza says so. The one exception: if one of them, or another company, has taken on the warranty in writing, that company is the one to claim from.
rules.what_you_get: You can ask the maker, the importer or the business that sold it to you to honour the warranty (the law names the producer, the importer and the distributor). It is done where you bought the item or where the póliza says. If you have to go anywhere else to get it done, they must cover what that costs you.
rules.how_to_claim: Start with the store where you bought it. If it tells you to go to the maker, say the law lets you claim from either of them and ask the store to deal with it. Put the request in writing and keep a dated copy. If nobody helps, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Article 79 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor lets me claim the warranty from the producer, the importer or the distributor, so I'm asking you to honour it here.
rules.source_quote: El cumplimiento de las garantías es exigible, indistintamente, al productor y al importador del bien o servicio, así como al distribuidor, salvo en los casos en que alguno de ellos o algún tercero asuma por escrito la obligación.

rules.title: Mexico: warranty small print can't take away your rights under the law
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. It applies to the terms of any warranty, whenever you make your claim.
rules.what_you_get: A warranty can't give you less than the law requires, and it can't add conditions or limits that cut the rights the law gives you. The consumer law can't be signed away either: no agreement, custom or practice can override it.
rules.how_to_claim: If the store points to a term in the póliza or on the receipt that limits what the law gives you, say in writing that article 79 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor bars warranty conditions that reduce your legal rights, and that article 1 says the law can't be waived. Then make your claim. If they won't budge, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Article 79 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor says a warranty can't set conditions that reduce my legal rights, so that condition doesn't apply to my claim.
rules.source_quote: Las garantías ofrecidas no pueden ser inferiores a las que determinen las disposiciones aplicables ni prescribir condiciones o limitaciones que reduzcan los derechos que legalmente corresponden al consumidor.

rules.title: Mexico: warranties on electronics and appliances cover every part, the labour and the shipping
rules.window_note: For as long as the warranty lasts: at least 3 months for electric and electronic products and at least 1 year for household appliances, or longer if the póliza says so. Shipping is covered when moving the product is needed to honour the warranty within the company's own service network.
rules.what_you_get: The warranty has to cover all the parts and components and include the labour. The maker or importer must replace any faulty part at no extra cost to you, and pay to move the product when that's needed to carry out the warranty within its service network.
rules.how_to_claim: Contact the service centre or maker named on the póliza. If they try to charge for a part, the labour or the transport, point to section 7.2 of NOM-024-SCFI-2013 and ask them to put any charge in writing. If they insist, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Under section 7.2 of NOM-024-SCFI-2013 the warranty covers all parts and labour, and the transport needed to honour it, so there should be no charge for this repair.
rules.source_quote: Las garantías deben amparar todas las piezas y componentes del producto e incluir la mano de obra. En consecuencia, los fabricantes nacionales e importadores están obligados a reemplazar cualquier pieza o componente defectuoso sin costo adicional para el consumidor.

rules.title: Mexico: an electronics or appliance warranty can only be refused for three reasons
rules.window_note: For as long as the warranty lasts: at least 3 months for electric and electronic products and at least 1 year for household appliances, or longer if the póliza says so.
rules.what_you_get: The maker, importer or seller can only get out of the warranty if you used the product in abnormal conditions, didn't use it the way the manual says, or had it altered or repaired by someone they hadn't authorised. Those exceptions must be clearly written in the póliza, or they can't rely on them. And they can't ask for more than the product plus the póliza stamped by the store, or the invoice or receipt that shows the product.
rules.how_to_claim: Bring the product with the stamped póliza, or the receipt that names the product. If they refuse for a reason that isn't one of the three, or one that isn't written in the póliza, say so and ask for the refusal in writing. Then call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Section 7.3 of NOM-024-SCFI-2013 only lets you refuse the warranty for abnormal use, not following the manual, or unauthorised repairs, and none of those happened here.
rules.source_quote: Los fabricantes nacionales, importadores o comercializadores responsables de los productos a los que se refiere esta Norma Oficial Mexicana, sólo pueden eximirse de hacer efectiva la garantía en los siguientes casos:

rules.title: Mexico: time in the repair shop doesn't count against your warranty
rules.window_note: Applies during the warranty: at least 90 days from delivery, or longer if the póliza says so. Every day the item spends in a warranty repair is added back on.
rules.what_you_get: The days a warranty repair takes don't count toward the warranty. Parts that were replaced start a warranty of their own, and the rest of the item keeps its original one. If you're given a replacement item instead, its warranty starts over.
rules.how_to_claim: Keep the service order that shows the day you dropped the item off and the day you got it back. If the store says the warranty has run out, add those days on and show them the new end date. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Under article 83 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor the time this spent in warranty repair doesn't count, so my warranty now runs until [date].
rules.source_quote: El tiempo que duren las reparaciones efectuadas al amparo de la garantía no es computable dentro del plazo de la misma.

rules.title: Mexico: bought by phone, mail order or online? The seller pays shipping for warranty repairs and returns
rules.window_note: For as long as the warranty lasts: at least 90 days from delivery, or longer if the póliza says so. The law names sales by phone, TV, mail or courier, or any other way where you never dealt with the seller in person; online shops likely count. The seller can make you pay only if you agreed to that, so check the terms you accepted.
rules.what_you_get: The seller covers transport and shipping when an item goes back for a repair or a return under the warranty. The seller also has to let you make claims and returns in a similar way to how you bought, for example online or by phone.
rules.how_to_claim: Contact the seller the same way you bought, through its website, app or phone line. Ask for a prepaid label or a pickup for the warranty repair or return, and name article 53. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Under article 53 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor the seller covers the shipping for warranty repairs and returns on a distance sale, so please send me a prepaid label or arrange a pickup.
rules.source_quote: Cubrir los costos de transporte y envío de mercancía en caso de haber devoluciones o reparaciones amparadas por la garantía, salvo pacto en contrario

rules.title: Mexico: if a warranty repair doesn't fix it, you can ask for a new one or your money back
rules.window_note: The item still doesn't work properly after a repair, inside the warranty (at least 90 days from delivery, or longer if the póliza says so). The law also says claims like this go in within 2 months of receiving the product, without saying whether a repaired item counts from when you got it back, so claim the day the repair turns out not to have worked.
rules.what_you_get: You choose: a replacement, which has to be new, or your money back when you hand the item over. With either one you also get a bonificación, a payment of at least 20% of the price you paid. A refund comes back the same way you paid unless you agree to something else.
rules.how_to_claim: Go back to the store, or to the maker or importer if you prefer; the law lets you pick. Say in writing that the repaired item still doesn't work and ask for a new replacement or a refund, plus the bonificación. They have 15 days to settle it. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722. For technical products, an expert or an accredited lab decides whether it works.
rules.script_hint: Article 92 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor says that if a repaired item still isn't fit to use within the warranty, I can choose a new replacement or a refund, plus a bonificación of at least 20% of the price.
rules.source_quote: Si el bien reparado no queda en estado adecuado para su uso o destino, dentro del plazo de garantía

rules.title: Mexico: 2 months to swap or return something that isn't the quality you were sold
rules.window_note: 2 months from the day you received it, as long as you didn't damage it. They can refuse if you're late, if you used it in ways it wasn't meant for, or if you caused serious damage that can't be fixed. For technical products, an expert or an accredited lab decides.
rules.what_you_get: If the item doesn't match the quality, brand or specifications it was sold with, or doesn't meet an official Mexican standard (NOM), you choose: a replacement, or your money back when you hand it over. Either way you also get a bonificación, a payment of at least 20% of the price. A refund comes back the same way you paid unless you agree to something else.
rules.how_to_claim: Within the 2 months, claim in writing from the store, the maker or the importer, whichever you choose. Bring the receipt and the ad, box or listing that shows what was promised. They have 15 days to settle it. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: This isn't the quality or specification it was sold with, so under articles 92 and 93 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor I'm asking for a replacement or a refund, plus a bonificación of at least 20% of the price.
rules.source_quote: Si el bien no corresponde a la calidad, marca, o especificaciones y demás elementos sustanciales bajo los cuales se haya ofrecido o no cumple con las normas oficiales mexicanas

rules.title: Mexico: a hidden defect gets you a swap, a refund or a lower price, plus at least 20%
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off in the article on hidden defects. The law's general limit for claims is one year (article 14), but it doesn't say which day that year starts, so claim as soon as you find the fault.
rules.what_you_get: If a hidden defect makes the item unfit for its normal use, lowers its quality or how well you can use it, or makes it less safe than you'd reasonably expect, you choose: have it restored or replaced (the law's word is restitución), cancel the sale and get your money back (plus interest in some cases), or keep it and pay less. With any of these you also get a bonificación of at least 20% of the price, and you can still claim for other losses it caused.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the store in writing what the defect is and which option you want, plus the bonificación. Keep the receipt and photos, or a technician's note, showing the fault. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: This has a hidden defect that makes it unfit for normal use, so under article 82 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor I'm asking for [a replacement / a refund / a lower price], plus a bonificación of at least 20% of the price.
rules.source_quote: El consumidor puede optar por pedir la restitución del bien o servicio, la rescisión del contrato o la reducción del precio, y en cualquier caso, la bonificación o compensación

rules.title: Mexico: makers must keep parts and repairs available while the product is still sold
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. It covers the warranty and then the whole time the product is still being made, assembled or distributed. After the warranty ends you pay for the repair; what the law guarantees is that parts and service are there.
rules.what_you_get: The maker has to make sure spare parts and a repair service are available in good time, during the warranty and for as long as the product is still being made, assembled or distributed.
rules.how_to_claim: Ask the maker in writing for the part or the repair, and name article 80 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor. If they say there are no parts while the model is still on sale, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Article 80 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor says you must supply parts and repair service while this product is still made or distributed, so please supply the part or the repair.
rules.source_quote: deberán asegurar y responder del suministro oportuno de partes y refacciones, así como del servicio de reparación, durante el término de vigencia de la garantía y, posteriormente, durante el tiempo en que los productos sigan fabricándose, armándose o distribuyéndose.

rules.title: Mexico: a repair that goes wrong within 90 days must be redone for free
rules.window_note: 90 calendar days from the day the repaired item was handed back to you, not from when you bought it. If the repair came with a longer warranty, the longer time counts. It covers faults caused by whoever did the repair or the maintenance.
rules.what_you_get: The repair or maintenance is done again at no cost to you.
rules.how_to_claim: Take it back to the same repair shop with the invoice or service note. Say the fault comes from their work and showed up within 90 days, and don't pay again. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: You repaired this less than 90 days ago and the fault comes from that repair, so under article 81 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor you have to redo it at no cost.
rules.source_quote: presente deficiencias imputables al autor de la reparación o del mantenimiento dentro de los noventa días naturales posteriores a la entrega del producto al consumidor, éste tendrá derecho a que sea reparado o mantenido de nuevo sin costo alguno.

rules.title: Mexico: a repair shop that loses or ruins your item owes you at least 20%
rules.window_note: This article sets no deadline of its own; the law's general limit for claims is one year. Claim as soon as you get the item back damaged, or learn it's been lost.
rules.what_you_get: If poor repair or maintenance work means your item is lost, or so damaged that it's no longer fit, fully or partly, for what it's for, the shop must pay you a bonificación of at least 20% of the price paid. You can still claim for your other losses on top; a court decides those.
rules.how_to_claim: Tell the shop in writing what happened and ask for the bonificación. Bring the service note or invoice, and photos. If they refuse, call Profeco on 800 468 8722.
rules.script_hint: Your repair work left my item [lost / unusable], so under article 61 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor you owe me a bonificación of at least 20% of the price paid.
rules.source_quote: deberán bonificar al consumidor en términos del artículo 92 TER si por deficiencia del servicio el bien se pierde o sufre tal deterioro que resulte total o parcialmente inapropiado para el uso a que esté destinado.

rules.title: Mexico: if you reported the fault before the warranty ended, Profeco can still take your claim
rules.window_note: Works after the warranty end date, as long as you can prove you went to the business while the warranty was still running. The law's general one-year limit on claims still applies.
rules.what_you_get: Your warranty claim doesn't die on the end date. You can bring it to Profeco afterwards if you can show you took it to the business in time.
rules.how_to_claim: Keep proof of the day you first reported the fault: a service order, a dated email or chat, or a report number. Take that proof, the póliza and the receipt to Profeco (800 468 8722, or a Profeco office) and file a complaint.
rules.script_hint: I reported this fault to you on [date], while the warranty was still running, so under article 84 of the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor my claim still stands.
rules.source_quote: Cuando el consumidor acuda a la Procuraduría para hacer valer sus derechos fuera del plazo establecido por la garantía, deberá acreditar que compareció ante el proveedor dentro del dicho plazo.

rules.title: Mexico: you have one year to claim, and a Profeco complaint stops the clock
rules.window_note: One year is the general limit for rights under the consumer law, unless the law sets another time; for example, 2 months to return something that isn't the quality you were sold. The law doesn't say which day the year starts, so don't wait. Once you file with Profeco, the clock stops for as long as the case runs.
rules.what_you_get: Up to one year to bring a claim under the consumer law. Filing a complaint with Profeco pauses the time limit on your legal claims for as long as the process lasts.
rules.how_to_claim: If the business says no, file with Profeco straight away: 800 468 8722, 55 5568 8722 in Mexico City, or a Profeco office. Keep a copy of your complaint with its date.
rules.script_hint: I'm within the one-year limit the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor gives me to claim (article 14), so I'd like you to deal with my claim.
rules.source_quote: El plazo de prescripción de los derechos y obligaciones establecidos en la presente ley será de un año, salvo otros términos previstos por esta ley.

rules.title: Mexico: Profeco will call the business in to try to settle your complaint
rules.window_note: No cut-off of its own. The law's general limit is one year, so file as soon as the business says no.
rules.what_you_get: Profeco checks your complaint and, if it's accepted, calls the business to a conciliation to reach a deal. That can end with your money back or a bonificación paid to you, among other outcomes. If there's no deal, Profeco can act as arbitrator if both sides agree; if not, you keep your right to go to court.
rules.how_to_claim: Pick one: a Profeco consumer office (ODECO) near you; Concilianet or Conciliaexprés online, which only work with companies registered on them; email asesoria@profeco.gob.mx; or the Teléfono del Consumidor, 800 468 8722 or 55 5568 8722. Have ready your name, address and official ID; the receipt, contract or invoice; the business's name and address; and a short account of what happened. In person, print and bring the complaint form (Formato de recepción de queja). You can ask for it to be handled where it happened, where you live or where the business is.
rules.script_hint: I'd like to settle this with you directly; if we can't, I'll ask Profeco to help us reach an agreement through its conciliation process.
rules.source_quote: Para ingresar una queja ante la Profeco, se cuenta con varias opciones: acudir a una de las 38 Oficinas de Defensa del Consumidor (ODECO) más cercana a su domicilio; a través de Concilianet y Conciliaexprés

rules.title: Ontario: a faulty item lets you claim the loss from the seller, or hand it back if you act early enough
rules.window_note: No fixed number of days. You can only hand it back before you have accepted it. You get a reasonable chance to check it first. You count as having accepted it once you tell the seller so, do something with it that only the owner could, or keep it for a reasonable time without saying you reject it. The Act also ends the right to hand it back once a particular item you picked out has become yours. For a sale with no conditions attached, that happens when the deal is made, so for an item taken off a store shelf it can be gone the moment you buy. The money claim stays either way. If you looked the item over, faults that look should have shown don't count against sellable quality. You have two years from when you found the problem to start a court case.
rules.what_you_get: If the item isn't of sellable quality, isn't reasonably fit for a purpose you made clear to the seller while relying on its judgment, or doesn't match its description, the seller has broken a condition of the sale. If you still have the right to reject it, you can hand it back and get your money back. Once that right is gone, the seller still owes you money for the loss the fault caused. For a quality fault that is, unless shown otherwise, the gap between what it was worth with the fault and what it would have been worth without it. You can take that off what you still owe, or sue for it.
rules.how_to_claim: As soon as you find the fault, tell the seller in writing what is wrong. If you haven't accepted the item yet, say you reject it and want your money back. If you've had it a while, or bought that exact item off the shelf, ask them instead to pay for the loss the fault caused; accepting a free repair or a swap is one way to settle it. If they refuse, file a free complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario, then go to Small Claims Court, which handles claims up to $50,000 and where you can act without a lawyer.
rules.script_hint: Ontario's Sale of Goods Act applies to my purchase, and this item wasn't of merchantable quality, so I'm asking for my money back or for you to cover what the fault has cost me.
rules.source_quote: the difference between the value of the goods at the time of delivery to the buyer and the value they would have had if they had answered to the warranty

rules.title: Ontario: if the seller misled you about what you bought, you can cancel within a year
rules.window_note: You must give notice within one year of the day you made the deal. Any form of notice works, as long as it says you want to cancel (or get money back) and why. It counts from the day you send it, so keep proof of that date. One false or misleading statement is enough.
rules.what_you_get: If the seller told you something false or misleading, such as that it was new when it was used or refurbished, that it was a model, grade or quality it isn't, that it had features it doesn't, that a part or repair was needed when it wasn't, or something untrue about the rights that come with the deal, you can cancel and get what you paid back, plus damages. If you can't give the item back, you can recover what you paid over what it was actually worth to you, or damages, or both. A court can add punitive damages.
rules.how_to_claim: Within the year, send the seller written notice that you are cancelling because of a false or misleading statement, and say what it was. If you don't get a satisfactory answer, you can sue: Small Claims Court handles up to $50,000 without a lawyer. You can also file a free complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario.
rules.script_hint: You told me this was [what they said], which wasn't true, so under section 18 of Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2002 I'm cancelling our agreement and asking for my money back.
rules.source_quote: Any agreement, whether written, oral or implied, entered into by a consumer after or while a person has engaged in an unfair practice may be rescinded by the consumer

rules.title: Ontario: car repairs come with 90 days or 5,000 km of cover on parts and labour
rules.window_note: 90 days or 5,000 km, whichever comes first, counted from the repair, not from when you bought the vehicle. So a repair done years after you bought it still gets its own cover. The garage can give you longer, and this sits on top of Ontario's other quality promises. You lose it on a part you misused or abused, but the garage needs reasonable grounds to say so.
rules.what_you_get: Every new or reconditioned part a garage puts in your vehicle, and the labour to put it in, is covered. If the repair fails and the vehicle can't be driven or isn't safe, and going back to the first garage isn't reasonable, you can have it fixed at the nearest place that can do it and claim back from the first garage what you paid for the original repair, plus reasonable towing.
rules.how_to_claim: Take the vehicle back to the garage that did the work, with the invoice, and ask them to fix it again at no charge under the repair warranty. If it broke down far away, get it fixed at the nearest shop, keep the old parts and all receipts, and ask the first garage in writing to repay you. If they refuse, file a free complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario, then Small Claims Court.
rules.script_hint: Section 63 of Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2002 covers the parts and labour on this repair for 90 days or 5,000 km, so I'm asking you to fix it again at no charge.
rules.source_quote: every repairer shall be deemed to warrant all new or reconditioned parts installed and the labour required to install them for a minimum of 90 days or 5,000 kilometres, whichever comes first

rules.title: Ontario: a job can't cost more than 10% over the estimate you were given
rules.window_note: Applies to any deal that came with an estimate, like a repair quote. If you asked for extra or different work, you and the business can agree a new price. If you already paid more than the law allows, you have one year from paying to demand the overcharge back; put it in writing so you can prove when you asked.
rules.what_you_get: The business can't charge more than the estimate plus 10%. If it does, you can make it do the job at the estimated price. For vehicle repairs a garage also can't charge for work you didn't approve, can't charge for the estimate unless it told you the fee up front, and can't charge for the estimate at all if you then let it do the work.
rules.how_to_claim: Before you pay, show the business the estimate and ask for the bill to be brought down to the estimated price. If you've already paid, write to them within a year asking for the overcharge back. If they refuse, file a free complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario, then Small Claims Court.
rules.script_hint: Section 10 of Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2002 says you can't charge more than 10% over the estimate, so I'm asking you to do this work at the estimated price.
rules.source_quote: If a consumer agreement includes an estimate, the supplier shall not charge the consumer an amount that exceeds the estimate by more than 10 per cent.

rules.title: Ontario: a repair or installation you pay for has to be done to an acceptable standard
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. The test is whether the work was of reasonably acceptable quality. You have two years from finding the problem to start a court case.
rules.what_you_get: Any service you pay a business for, such as a repair, an installation or a setup, comes with a legal promise that it is of reasonably acceptable quality. A contract term that tries to cancel or water down that promise is void. If the work falls short, the business has broken that promise and you can claim what it cost you.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the business, say what went wrong with the work, and ask them to put it right at no charge or pay you back. If they won't, file a free complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario, then go to Small Claims Court for up to $50,000 without a lawyer.
rules.script_hint: Section 9 of Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2002 says your service had to be of reasonably acceptable quality, and this work wasn't, so please put it right at no cost to me.
rules.source_quote: The supplier is deemed to warrant that the services supplied under a consumer agreement are of a reasonably acceptable quality.

rules.title: Ontario: the province can try to settle it with the business, for free
rules.window_note: It may not be able to help if what happened was more than two years ago. The ministry recommends telling the business about the problem first. After you file, it says it will contact you within 15 business days.
rules.what_you_get: Consumer Protection Ontario, run by the provincial ministry, takes complaints about businesses that break Ontario's consumer laws, at no cost to you. It may try to settle things between you and the business, or send you to the right office; some areas, like car dealerships, travel and home builders, are handled elsewhere. It mainly helps with getting back money you paid or cancelling an agreement, not other damages, and not quality problems beyond the basic legal guarantees.
rules.how_to_claim: First write to the business (letter or email) saying what went wrong and what you want; if you call, note the date and what was said. If they don't fix it, file online on ontario.ca, or email the form to consumer@ontario.ca, with your letter, their reply, your receipt or contract and payment records. If that doesn't settle it, Small Claims Court handles claims up to $50,000 without a lawyer.
rules.script_hint: I've told you about this problem and it hasn't been fixed, so I'll be filing a complaint with Consumer Protection Ontario unless we can sort it out this week.
rules.source_quote: If the business does not resolve your complaint after receiving your letter, email, or phone call, you can file a complaint with us.

rules.title: Ontario: fine print can't stop you taking a business to court
rules.window_note: Applies whatever the contract or terms of service say. Once a dispute has started you can still choose arbitration if you want to.
rules.what_you_get: Your rights under Ontario's Consumer Protection Act apply even if you signed or clicked something that says otherwise. A clause that says disputes must go to private arbitration can't stop you from suing under the Act, and a clause that bans class actions doesn't stop you from joining one.
rules.how_to_claim: If a business points to an arbitration or no-class-action clause, tell them in writing that sections 7 and 8 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2002 make it invalid against you, and carry on with your claim: first the business, then a free complaint to Consumer Protection Ontario, then court.
rules.script_hint: Section 7 of Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2002 means your arbitration clause can't stop me from taking this to court.
rules.source_quote: any term or acknowledgment in a consumer agreement or a related agreement that requires or has the effect of requiring that disputes arising out of the consumer agreement be submitted to arbitration is invalid

rules.title: Quebec: for a hidden defect, the store and the maker can't say they didn't know
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off in the Consumer Protection Act. It only covers a defect you couldn't have spotted with an ordinary look when you bought it. Raise it as soon as you find it.
rules.what_you_get: If the item had a hidden defect, you can claim directly from the store or from the manufacturer. Neither one can defend itself by saying it didn't know about the defect. The same goes if the item came without the safety instructions you needed to avoid a danger you wouldn't otherwise know about.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the store, the manufacturer, or both. Describe the defect, say it couldn't be seen when you bought it, and ask for a repair, a replacement or your money back. If they refuse, send a formal notice with a deadline, call the OPC for free advice, then file at the Small Claims Division of the Court of Québec, which hears claims up to $15,000 with no lawyers.
rules.script_hint: Section 53 of Quebec's Consumer Protection Act lets me claim from you directly for this hidden defect, and you can't rely on not having known about it, so please repair, replace or refund it.
rules.source_quote: The merchant or the manufacturer shall not plead that he was unaware of the defect or lack of instructions.

rules.title: Quebec: bought it second-hand? The maker still has to stand behind it
rules.window_note: No fixed cut-off. It's the same 'reasonable time' test as for the first owner, judged on the price, the terms of the sale and how the item was used. This right is against the manufacturer; to claim from a store, you need to have bought from that store.
rules.what_you_get: If you're not the first owner, you can still go straight to the manufacturer when the item has a hidden defect, isn't fit for normal use, didn't last a reasonable time, or its parts and repairs aren't available. And under a written warranty, the store or maker can't make you prove that earlier owners followed the warranty's conditions.
rules.how_to_claim: Write to the manufacturer's customer service. Say you're a later owner, describe the problem, and ask for a repair, a replacement or a refund under sections 53 and 54 of Quebec's Consumer Protection Act. If they refuse, send a formal notice, call the OPC, then use the Small Claims Division of the Court of Québec (up to $15,000, no lawyers).
